$scopeNote: Only ORDINARY (consumer/creditor judgment) wage garnishment is state-overridable here. Federal law — support orders, federal tax levies, federal student loan default — preempts a state's own wage-exemption statute entirely, so nothing in this file ever changes those two calculations in src/garnishment.ts; only 'consumer_creditor' orders consult it. A state absent from this file entirely has no known departure from the plain federal CCPA default and is computed with it as-is — a narrower claim than 'every state's garnishment law has been fully researched.' A state PRESENT in this file with only a `knownGap` note (no `ordinaryGarnishmentProhibited`/`ordinaryGarnishment`/`headOfFamilyOrdinaryGarnishment`/`fullExemption` block) means a real departure IS known to exist but isn't modelled yet — also computed against the federal default in the meantime, but disclosed rather than silent. 16 states now carry a modelled override; 2 more (NJ, MD) are flagged known-but-unmodelled; the remaining 32 + DC are the unconfirmed-federal-default baseline described above.

sources.title: Minn. Stat. § 571.922 — non-support garnishment: fully exempt at or below 40x the applicable minimum wage; 10% between 40x-60x; 15% between 60x-80x; 25% above 80x (a cliff schedule — crossing a threshold puts the WHOLE disposable-earnings figure in that bracket, not just the excess, unlike the federal formula)
sources.verifiedBy: Directly fetched. Confirmed the threshold-cliff (not marginal) structure explicitly, the 3 percentage tiers and their multiplier boundaries, and that the statute uses the greater of Minnesota's own minimum wage (Minn. Stat. 177.24) or the federal FLSA minimum wage.

NY.$note: New York sets a REGIONAL minimum wage — $17.00/hr for NYC, Long Island and Westchester vs. $16.00/hr for the rest of the state — but this engine's workState is a bare 2-letter code with no county/region granularity to key off. stateMinimumHourlyWage here uses the LOWER, statewide-outside-downstate figure ($16.00) as a documented simplification: for an employee actually working in the $17.00 region, the true 30x floor is higher than this computes, meaning this engine could compute a small garnishment where the true NYC/LI/Westchester floor would still protect it entirely. This is a genuine, disclosed gap, not an assumed-safe direction — same disclosure discipline as this project's other geographic-granularity gaps (see docs/geocoding-coverage.md).

WA.$note: Washington's own minimum wage is keyed by STATE law only for this statute (not 'greater of state or federal') and already far exceeds the federal $7.25, so the federal figure never enters this calculation at all. Washington's statute is unusual among the states in this file for naming a THIRD category (private student loans, 15%/50x) this engine doesn't separately represent — a private (non-federal) student loan default would need its own GarnishmentOrderType to model correctly; only the federal student loan default program (34 CFR 34.19) is modelled anywhere in this project today.

sources.title: Nev. Rev. Stat. § 31.295 — sliding-scale ordinary garnishment: 18% of disposable earnings if gross weekly pay is $770 or less, 25% if it exceeds $770; either way also capped at the amount by which disposable earnings exceed 50x the FEDERAL minimum hourly wage (not a 'greater of state or federal' test — the statute's own floor names the federal figure specifically)
sources.verifiedBy: Cross-source confirmed via search synthesis quoting the statute's own $770 gross-weekly breakpoint, the 18%/25% tiers, and the 50x-FEDERAL-minimum-wage floor specifically (not Nevada's own, notably higher, minimum wage), not an independently rendered direct fetch this pass.

NV.$note: Unlike every OTHER tiered/bracket state in this file, Nevada's own breakpoint ($770) is a FIXED GROSS-WEEKLY DOLLAR FIGURE, not indexed to any minimum wage — and the tier decides the FRACTION while that fraction is then applied to DISPOSABLE earnings, not gross. This is genuinely a different mechanism from Minnesota's minimum-wage-indexed cliff tiers (see GarnishmentGrossWeeklyTier's own doc comment in src/registry.ts), which is why this engine represents it as a separate shape rather than reusing `tiers`. $770 is a nominal dollar figure fixed by the statute's own text, not something that moves with inflation on its own — re-verify it hasn't been amended when this file rolls forward, rather than assuming it scales like the minimum-wage-based floors elsewhere in this file do.

sources.title: Haw. Rev. Stat. § 652-1 — MARGINAL brackets on monthly disposable earnings: 5% of the first $100/month, 10% of the next $100/month (i.e. the $100-$200 slice), 20% of everything over $200/month, prorated to 'an equivalent portion... per week' for other pay frequencies
sources.verifiedBy: Cross-source confirmed via search synthesis quoting the statute's own 5%/10%/20% figures and its $100/$200 monthly breakpoints, not an independently rendered direct fetch this pass.

HI.$note: This is the only MARGINAL (income-tax-bracket-style) garnishment formula in this file — every other tiered state here (Minnesota, Nevada) uses a CLIFF where crossing a threshold reclassifies the WHOLE amount, not just the slice above it. The $100/$200 monthly breakpoints are small, fixed nominal-dollar figures with no visible minimum-wage or inflation indexing in the sources reviewed — they read as though they may not have been updated in a long time, but this file models the statute as currently written rather than adjusting it. No separate minimum-wage floor is layered on top; none was found in the sources reviewed.

sources.title: Mo. Rev. Stat. § 525.030 — a head-of-family debtor's ordinary (non-support) garnishment is capped at the lesser of 10% of disposable earnings or the amount by which disposable earnings exceed 30x the FEDERAL minimum hourly wage; a non-head-of-family debtor gets the plain federal 25%/30x default
sources.verifiedBy: Cross-source confirmed via search synthesis quoting the statute's own head-of-family 10%/30x variant and confirming the non-head-of-family case matches the plain federal default, not an independently rendered direct fetch this pass.

MO.$note: Distinct from Florida's `fullExemption`: a Missouri head-of-family debtor still owes something (10% of disposable earnings), just at a reduced rate from the ordinary 25% — never a full $0 regardless of income. Missouri's own statute also names a 50%-of-disposable-earnings figure for a head-of-family debtor when the UNDERLYING DEBT ITSELF is for the support of another person — not modelled here, because this engine already routes any support-related withholding through the separate `child_support` order type and its own federal 50/55/60/65% ceilings rather than through `consumer_creditor` at all, so that branch of 525.030 has no code path that would ever reach it.

sources.title: N.J. Stat. Ann. § 2A:17-56 — wage execution limited to 10% of income when the debtor earns at or below 250% of the federal poverty level for their household size; up to 25% of gross above that threshold (higher still for debts owed to the State)
sources.verifiedBy: Cross-source confirmed via search synthesis quoting the statute's own income-tier mechanism, not an independently rendered direct fetch this pass.

NJ.knownGap: New Jersey's own cap is keyed to the debtor's income AS A FRACTION OF THE FEDERAL POVERTY GUIDELINE FOR THEIR HOUSEHOLD SIZE — a real, confirmed departure from every other state in this file, but one this engine cannot compute today: nothing in PaycheckInput or GarnishmentOrder carries household size, and HHS's poverty guideline table itself is a separate, annually-published figure this project doesn't otherwise track anywhere. Not modelled; New Jersey computes against the plain federal default in the meantime, which is very likely WRONG for a debtor near or below the 250%-of-poverty line (federal 25% where NJ law would actually cap at 10%).

sources.title: Md. Code, Com. Law § 15-601.1 — the statewide default tracks the federal formula, but several Maryland COUNTIES (and Caroline County by a separate provision) set their own lower percentage caps for ordinary garnishment by local law
sources.verifiedBy: Cross-source confirmed via search synthesis describing the county-level variation, not an independently rendered direct fetch of the statute or any specific county's own ordinance this pass — no attempt was made to enumerate which counties diverge or by how much.

MD.knownGap: Maryland's garnishment cap varies by COUNTY, not just by state — this engine's workState is state-level only and carries no county, so a genuine local departure can't be looked up even in principle without first threading county-level geography into GarnishmentInput the way geocode/ already does for local income tax. Not modelled; Maryland computes against the plain federal default in the meantime. Same structural shape as this project's other sub-state-geography gaps (Ohio JEDD/JEDZ, Pennsylvania Act 32) — the difference is those are already wired end-to-end and this one isn't yet.
